title: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
hook: the handoff: the plan is tidy, and the next person might change half of it
carry: karma: a service capstone — a year designed and reviewed
tomorrow: why would God want to know what loving God feels like?

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma without fever: own the fix, drop the trophy and the sentence. Today, the capstone's last day, and a handoff.

The handoff doc is finished. The notes are tidy, every reason written down. Then the person taking over reads it and says, thanks, I might change some of this. There's a word on the tip of the tongue, and it's: don't. The Bhagavad Gita ends near a moment a lot like that. Between two armies, Krishna has taught Arjuna for chapters and made his whole case. And then he hands Arjuna something a reader might not expect from a teacher who's just won the argument.
screen: `THE HANDOFF DOC IS DONE.` → `I MIGHT CHANGE SOME OF THIS.` → `WHAT DOES KRISHNA HAND OVER?`

segments.voice: Near the end, Krishna says, in paraphrase: I've told you this wisdom, more secret than any secret. Reflect on it fully. Then do as you wish. No order. The choice, handed back. Arjuna's answer comes a few verses later: my confusion is gone, my memory has come back, I stand firm, my doubts are gone, and I'll do as you say. Notice the order. Reflection first, then a free yes. A yes that was ordered wouldn't be the same yes. That's the capstone's last move, and not an easy one. A year of service, designed and reviewed, ends by being handed on. The designer explains the reasons fully: why the pace is measured, why the gifts are quiet, why the review asks about others. Then lets the next person choose. Some of the plan will change. The teacher in the Gita seems to take that risk on purpose, because what he's after isn't obedience. It's understanding that chooses. Readers hear the verse in more than one way: some as real freedom given to Arjuna, some as a teacher's trust that full reflection will lead one way. Both keep the same order. Think it through, then choose. And the capstone comes full circle. It began with the work already on the calendar. It ends with the work in someone else's hands.
screen: `REFLECT FULLY, THEN DO AS YOU WISH.` · `CONFUSION GONE. A FREE YES.` · `EXPLAIN, THEN HAND IT ON.` · then, large: `UNDERSTANDING THAT CHOOSES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Bring to mind one thing you're about to pass on: a job, a habit, a recipe, a piece of advice. On each out-breath, loosen your grip on how it has to turn out, and rest in having explained it well.
Karma, handed on: work explained fully, then given over to someone else's free choice.
Hold onto this: karma, a year designed and reviewed, then handed on. The capstone is complete.

screen: `DAY 1657 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHY WOULD GOD WANT TO KNOW?`

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers point to Gita 18.63 when they speak of teaching: the student is given reasons and asked to reflect, and the choice is left to them.

fork.setup: you're teaching your little brother a family recipe, and he wants to add chili to it. what does Gita 18.63 suggest?
options: tell him why it's made this way, then let him decide.
forbid it. a recipe handed down shouldn't change.
let him do anything, and skip the explaining.
fork.reveal: Krishna gives his reasons in full, then says: do as you wish. the free yes, or the free change, comes after understanding.

original.note: Sanskrit, from Gita 18.63: as you wish, so do. Krishna's words after reflect on it fully.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher's job is to get you to obey.
what it means: Krishna gives his reasons, then hands Arjuna the choice; the yes that follows is free.
what a scholar hears: Gita 18.63, vimrishyaitad asheshena yathecchasi tatha kuru; and 18.73, nashto mohah smritir labdha.
